entry.title: Breaking the OOM Barrier: High-Rank Multi-Dimensional Sparse Einsum via Compressed Sparse Fiber (CSF) on GPU

link.title: Breaking the OOM Barrier: High-Rank Multi-Dimensional Sparse Einsum via Compressed Sparse Fiber (CSF) on GPU

entry.content:
Einstein Summation (einsum) is arguably the most expressive and pervasive primitive within the artificial intelligence field. From matrix multiplications and tensor contractions to the orchestration of complex batched attention mechanisms in Transformers, einsum acts as a domain-specific language that rules them all. As Tim Rocktäschel famously stated, “einsum is all you need”. It allows developers to write clean, declarative multi-dimensional array operations that can be automatically compiled and optimized down to hardware-level kernels.

However, when deep learning models confront massive, high-dimensional datasets with structural sparsity—such as user-item-word recommendation graphs, electronic medical records, or cybersecurity network logs—the standard execution routes offered by industry-leading frameworks break down completely.

This post analyzes the severe architectural limitations of PyTorch and TensorFlow when handling high-rank sparse einsum expressions, introduces the Compressed Sparse Fiber (CSF) representation, and exhibits how a custom-designed, memory-compact CUDA engine (Paramoneur) can outperform standard frameworks by orders of magnitude.

1. The Densification Trap: PyTorch & TensorFlow Deficiencies

While PyTorch and TensorFlow offer high-performance dense einsum solvers backed by backend utilities like NVIDIA cuTENSOR and cuBLAS, their sparse tensor support is tightly restricted. At present, neither framework can compute generic high-rank sparse-sparse contractions natively. If you pass an expression like "abcde,bdace->abe" using sparse formats, the engines will throw a NotImplementedError or force you to explicitly execute a conversion layer via .to_dense() or tf.sparse.to_dense().

For small arrays, this conversion layer goes unnoticed. But when working with large multi-way datasets spanning big dimensions—for instance, a geometry space of [50x50x50x20x10]—the memory footprint escalates exponentially. Storing this space in a dense layout demands an allocation of: \(\text{Total Elements} = 50 \times 50 \times 50 \times 20 \times 10 = 25,000,000 \text{ float elements}\)

If the dimensionality scales up further to high-order tensors, a dense matrix layout will immediately trigger a catastrophic Out-Of-Memory (OOM) hardware crash.

Why the Standard Coordinate (COO) Layout Fails for Contractions

To circumvent dense memory limits, developers turn to sparse representations, where the Coordinate (COO) layout is the most ubiquitous default. A COO tensor isolates only the non-zero elements (NNZ) by tracking a flat value array along with a multi-row index grid where every element’s precise coordinates are explicitly stated.

While COO is ideal for basic operations like sparse matrix-vector additions, executing a multi-axis einsum contraction on a raw COO layout becomes a performance nightmare. Because the structural non-zeros are scattered throughout the coordinate list, calculating an intersection or a matching index along a contracted axis requires a full Cartesian Cross-Product of the element sheets, yielding an algorithmic complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\text{NNZ}_A \times \text{NNZ}_B)$.

At an NNZ of $100,000$ items, a raw COO contraction requires the GPU to schedule and trace $100,000 \times 100,000 = 10 \text{ billion}$ individual comparison checks. This unstructured memory access pattern causes immense thread divergence, destroys cache locality, and saturates the VRAM memory bandwidth with redundant, non-coalesced read cycles.

2. Introducing Compressed Sparse Fiber (CSF)

To solve the structural limitations of multi-dimensional sparse data, Smith, Park, and Karypis introduced the Compressed Sparse Fiber (CSF) data structure. CSF is the multi-dimensional generalization of the popular Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) matrix format, recursively compressing each mode of a sparse tensor into a set of prefix trees.

Formal Definition

A sparse tensor $\mathcal{X}$ of order M is represented in CSF by recursively isolating unique coordinates across successive hierarchical modes. Structurally, it eliminates coordinate redundancy by encoding paths from a root node down to leaf levels, where each complete path represents an active non-zero element. It is implemented via three contiguously allocated arrays:

  1. vals: A flat array storing the non-zero values located at the leaf level.
  2. fids: Stores the explicit coordinate label of each node at every level of the tree.
  3. fptr: A sequence of M row-pointer arrays where each array segment acts as an indexing boundaries map into the next mode level, with the final pointer array mapping directly into the leaf non-zeros.
[Mode 0: i]   ->  Unique 'i' coordinates
                     |   (fptr defines boundaries)
[Mode 1: j]   ->  Unique 'j' children for each 'i'
                     |   (fptr defines boundaries)
[Mode 2: k]   ->  Leaves holding the sparse values

By organizing the multi-way data hierarchically, CSF reveals massive opportunities for computational and bandwidth savings. If multiple non-zero items share common ancestors (such as a shared prefix (i, j)), the tensor contraction engine can compute the overlapping subset of products once, bringing the contributions up and down the tree branches recursively. This fiber-centric traversal replaces the expensive linear search loops with focused tree lookups, reducing the number of sparse matrix row accesses dramatically.

Despite its overwhelming performance benefits for data-intensive machine learning workloads, neither PyTorch nor TensorFlow implements the CSF data structure natively. Both frameworks remain anchored to flat matrices or loose COO layouts, motivating the critical need to build custom, highly optimized acceleration libraries.

Core Architecture of the Multi-Dimensional CUDA Intersection Kernel

To achieve sub-millisecond execution times without the massive memory overhead of dense matrices, the launch_csf_einsum_two_tensors engine shifts the parallel computing paradigm from a blind matrix multiplication to a streamlined, multi-dimensional coordinate intersection. The codebase is available here.

The underlying CUDA kernel abandons the standard 2D grid allocation pattern (NNZ_A x NNZ_B), which triggers massive thread explosion and hardware-level warp scheduler stall. Instead, it linearizes the execution grid into a clean 1D configuration, allocating exactly one CUDA thread per structural non-zero entry of the first sparse tensor operator (csf_A.nnz).

The precise mathematical execution steps performed concurrently by each active GPU thread map directly to the hardware registers as follows:

  1. Coalesced Ancestor Fetching: The thread utilizes its global identifier (blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x) to read its own multidimensional coordinate tuple out of csf_A.d_coordinate_matrix in a single coalesced transaction, caching the entries into a static register array (coords_A).
  2. Permuted Target Realignment: Before executing any search passes, the thread maps the data layout of A into the exact lessicographical ordering required by B. By looking up the global metadata stored in the execution plan (plan.map_B_to_global), it rearranges its own elements into a secondary, short register vector (target_B_coords) corresponding to the permuted axis sequence of the second operator (e.g., mapping a raw layout of [a,b,c,d,e] into the target layout [b,d,a,c,e]).
  3. Logarithmic Binary Matching: Since the data loader forces a rigid, bitwise sorted alignment on the second operator in VRAM, the thread executes a highly optimized Binary Search (while (low <= high)) across csf_B.d_coordinate_matrix. At each step, a fast mid-point lessicographical comparison (compare_coordinates) evaluates the unified 64-bit key layouts against target_B_coords, isolating the exact structural intersection match in at most $\log_2(NNZ_B)$ iterations.
  4. Isolated Atomic Reduction: If a coordinate intersection is found, the thread pulls the floating-point values from both unifed memory spaces, multiplies them, and performs a thread-safe atomicAdd on the global counter. The final step projescts the active dimensions out to the contiguous UnifiedCOOOutput slots, selectively dropping the contracted indexes and outputting a single, reduced record onto the GPU.

3. High-Performance CUDA Design: Zero-Allocation In-Place Conversion

Implementing an arbitrary, high-rank sparse einsum on GPU requires a fine-grained, parallel approach. In our custom system, Paramoneur, we map exactly one CUDA thread to every active non-zero element of the input tensor. By sorting the target array lexicographically using an efficient bitwise pre-pass, each thread can find its precise coordinate intersections using a fast Binary Search over the second sparse operator. This drops the computational complexity from a blinding $\mathcal{O}(\text{NNZ}_A \times \text{NNZ}_B)$ down to $\mathcal{O}(\text{NNZ}_A \log(\text{NNZ}_B))$.

The results are initially written into a compact Coordinate (COO) output buffer. To protect the GPU from Out-Of-Memory exceptions, we consolidate the output arrays—allocating indices, floating values, and the global atomic counter—into a single, contiguous block of VRAM using Pointer Arithmetic.

[ Unified Output Buffer Space ]
+----------------------------+-----------------------+---------------+

| d_out_indices (ints)       | d_out_vals (floats)   | atomic_counter|
+----------------------------+-----------------------+---------------+
^                            ^                       ^
base_ptr                     + indices_bytes         + vals_bytes

In-Place Transformation into CSF

To completely minimize the memory footprint, we must avoid allocating a separate, secondary block of memory when converting the resulting COO back into a compressed CSF tree structure. Because an einsum contraction naturally reduces the dimensionality of the tensor via axis summation, the number of unique non-zero entries in the output is mathematically guaranteed to be smaller than or equal to the maximum capacity allocated for the intermediate COO buffer ($NNZ_{out} \le NNZ_{max}$).

We exploit this vacant space at runtime to perform an In-Place CSF Conversion directly within the VRAM buffer:

  1. We use a specialized CUDA compression kernel to scan the sorted d_out_indices and detect structural boundaries where coordinates change.
  2. The flat d_out_vals are shifted in-place to align with the new leaf nodes without colliding with other registers.
  3. The remaining unutilized memory slots at the tail end of the unifed buffer are recycled as a Scratchpad Space to lay down the hierarchical d_all_ptrs segmentation arrays.

By restructuring the pointers internally, a single cudaFree on the base buffer pointer releases both the intermediate COO arrays and the final compiled UniversalCSF tree object simultaneously, bringing the net memory allocation cost down to zero.

4. Parallelizing the Data Loader on the CPU

Even with lightning-fast GPU kernels, the entire pipeline will stutter if loading raw COO arrays from file systems into VRAM is executed sequentially on a single CPU core. To maximize the input data-loading throughput, we must offload the bottleneck of sorting and data preparation onto the GPU.

Instead of running a heavy std::sort on the host, the data loader can execute a fast, parallel Bitwise Radix Sort using NVIDIA Thrust:

  1. Flat Row-Major Compacting: During the raw text file stream, every incoming multidimensional coordinate is immediately packed into a single 64-bit unsigned integer (uint64_t) by allocating a fixed bit-width per dimension (e.g., 6 bits per axis allows mapping coordinate spaces up to 63 without overlap).
  2. Thrust Radix Sort: The raw, un-ordered values and their compact 64-bit keys are shipped directly via a PCIe bulk transfer to the GPU. We then invoke thrust::sort_by_key, which triggers the underlying CUB hardware-level radix sort across thousands of CUDA cores simultaneously.
  3. Parallel Bitwise Unpack: A simple, custom CUDA kernel reads the sorted keys and executes an inverse bitwise shift (>>) to populate the final d_coordinate_matrix instantaneously, cutting data-loading latencies down to a fraction of a millisecond.

5. Experimental Replicability & Performance Analysis

To validate the scalability of our custom framework against standard industry solutions, we configure an identical, high-rank 5D tensor contraction problem using the expression "abcde,bdace->abe" across an extensive range of non-zero intensities (NNZ).

The following scripts allow full replicability of the data generation and the framework comparison benchmarks.

A. Data Generation Script (generate_data.py)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import os

os.makedirs("benchmark_data", exist_ok=True)
DIM_A, DIM_B, DIM_C, DIM_D, DIM_E = 50, 50, 50, 20, 10
shape = (DIM_A, DIM_B, DIM_C, DIM_D, DIM_E)
shape2 = (DIM_B, DIM_D, DIM_A, DIM_C, DIM_E)
nnz_steps = [1, 10, 100, 1000, 100000, 500000]

np.random.seed(42)
print("=== Generating Sparse Datasets ===")

for nnz in nnz_steps:
    coordsA = set()
    coordsB = set()
    while len(coordsA) < nnz:
        coordsA.add((np.random.randint(0, shape[0]), np.random.randint(0, shape[1]), 
                     np.random.randint(0, shape[2]), np.random.randint(0, shape[3]), 
                     np.random.randint(0, shape[4])))
        coordsB.add((np.random.randint(0, shape2[0]), np.random.randint(0, shape2[1]), 
                     np.random.randint(0, shape2[2]), np.random.randint(0, shape2[3]), 
                     np.random.randint(0, shape2[4])))

    dfA = pd.DataFrame(np.array(list(coordsA)))
    dfA['value'] = np.random.rand(nnz) * 10.0
    dfA.to_csv(f"benchmark_data/tensor_A_{nnz}.csv", index=False, header=False)

    dfB = pd.DataFrame(np.array(list(coordsB)))
    dfB['value'] = 2.0
    dfB.to_csv(f"benchmark_data/tensor_B_{nnz}.csv", index=False, header=False)
print("[SUCCESS] Datasets written into benchmark_data/")

B. PyTorch & TensorFlow Scalability Script (benchmark_sota.py)

import torch
import tensorflow as tf
import pandas as pd
import time
import csv

DIM_A, DIM_B, DIM_C, DIM_D, DIM_E = 50, 50, 50, 20, 10
shapeA = (DIM_A, DIM_B, DIM_C, DIM_D, DIM_E)
shapeB = (DIM_B, DIM_D, DIM_A, DIM_C, DIM_E)
nnz_steps = [1, 10, 100, 1000, 100000, 500000]

with open("benchmark_frameworks_scalability.csv", mode="w", newline="") as log_file:
    writer = csv.writer(log_file)
    writer.writerow(["Framework", "NNZ", "Tempo_Mutazione_ms", "Tempo_Algebra_ms"])

    for nnz in nnz_steps:
        df_A = pd.read_csv(f"benchmark_data/tensor_A_{nnz}.csv", header=None)
        df_B = pd.read_csv(f"benchmark_data/tensor_B_{nnz}.csv", header=None)

        coords_A, vals_A = df_A.iloc[:, 0:5].values, df_A.iloc[:, 5].values
        coords_B, vals_B = df_B.iloc[:, 0:5].values, df_B.iloc[:, 5].values

        # --- PYTORCH ---
        start_mut = time.perf_counter_ns()
        pt_indices_A = torch.tensor(coords_A, dtype=torch.long).t().cuda()
        pt_values_A = torch.tensor(vals_A, dtype=torch.float32).cuda()
        pt_indices_B = torch.tensor(coords_B, dtype=torch.long).t().cuda()
        pt_values_B = torch.tensor(vals_B, dtype=torch.float32).cuda()
        T_A_pt = torch.sparse_coo_tensor(pt_indices_A, pt_values_A, shapeA).to_dense()
        T_B_pt = torch.sparse_coo_tensor(pt_indices_B, pt_values_B, shapeB).to_dense()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        t_mut_pt = (time.perf_counter_ns() - start_mut) / 1_000_000

        start_alg = time.perf_counter_ns()
        risultato_torch = torch.einsum("abcde,bdace->abe", T_A_pt, T_B_pt)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        t_alg_pt = (time.perf_counter_ns() - start_alg) / 1_000_000
        writer.writerow(["PyTorch", nnz, f"{t_mut_pt:.6f}", f"{t_alg_pt:.6f}"])

        # --- TENSORFLOW ---
        start_mut = time.perf_counter_ns()
        T_A_tf = tf.sparse.to_dense(tf.sparse.SparseTensor(coords_A, vals_A, shapeA))
        T_B_tf = tf.sparse.to_dense(tf.sparse.SparseTensor(coords_B, vals_B, shapeB))
        t_mut_tf = (time.perf_counter_ns() - start_mut) / 1_000_000

        start_alg = time.perf_counter_ns()
        risultato_tf = tf.einsum("abcde,bdace->abe", T_A_tf, T_B_tf)
        t_alg_tf = (time.perf_counter_ns() - start_alg) / 1_000_000
        writer.writerow(["TensorFlow", nnz, f"{t_mut_tf:.6f}", f"{t_alg_tf:.6f}"])

Analysis of the Experimental Benchmarks

The empirical results collected from the scalability execution trace display a massive, undeniable gap in architectural behavior:

Critical Takeaways

  1. The Mutation Overhead: For PyTorch and TensorFlow, the Transformation phase encompasses allocating a multi-dimensional matrix and filling it up completely via .to_dense(). At a high NNZ count of $100,000$, TensorFlow demands a staggering $31.802096 \text{ ms}$ just to prepare the dense target buffer space. Our custom library, Paramoneur, parallelizes coordinate parsing using GPU Radix Sort, completing the entire buffer construction and pointer layout mapping in a crisp $3.817380 \text{ ms}$.
  2. Algebra Performance: Once the matrices are densified, TensorFlow’s einsum is remarkably fast ($0.880244 \text{ ms}$ at $100,000$ items) due to its utilization of NVIDIA’s specialized core-level dense GEMM routines. However, Paramoneur matches this performance natively on purely sparse structures, executing the contraction in $0.218112 \text{ ms}$ without ever consuming the massive, dangerous footprint required by a dense matrix.
  3. The Core Limitation Revealed: The steady, flat times exhibited by PyTorch and TensorFlow across varying NNZ counts clarify that their execution speed is bound exclusively to the maximum dimensions of the dense shape, totally disregarding the actual sparse density of the problem. As a consequence, if the tensor’s shape increases slightly further, PyTorch and TensorFlow will hit a memory wall and crash, whereas our CSF-based engine scales gracefully alongside the actual data complexity.

6. Conclusions

The experimental evidence remarks a deep architectural limitation within mainstream frameworks: PyTorch and TensorFlow treat sparse tensors as low-level commodities, forcing memory-destructive densification layers whenever a high-rank complex contraction is requested.

By building custom frameworks that leverage the formal principles of Compressed Sparse Fiber (CSF) structures coupled with single-allocation pointer arithmetic and bitwise radix sorting, developers can completely shatter the OOM barrier. Paramoneur proves that it is entirely possible to compute multi-axis contractions with sub-millisecond execution times, combining the memory efficiency of sparse representations with the raw, uncapped speed of dedicated GPU hardware.

entry.title: High-Performance Context Management in Yaucl
entry.content:
Codebase: https://github.com/LogDS/yaucl/tree/master/include/yaucl/structures/gamma_context

1. Theoretical Computer Science Context and the Problem of Replicated Environments

In programming language theory, type-checkers, compilers, and constraint solvers must continuously track a formal context—traditionally denoted as $\Gamma$. This context maps identifiers to their types, variable definitions, or active constraints. As an interpreter evaluates deep reduction branches, type-checks polymorphic terms, or executes backtracking search loops, it creates a massive number of nested sub-contexts derived from a root environment.

Each evaluation branch requires an isolated view of $\Gamma$ where it can freely insert new definitions, override (shadow) existing variables, or reorder elements. Implementing this with standard containers (std::unordered_map coupled with a sequential std::list) forces the engine to clone the entire container at every branching point. This traditional approach introduces severe hardware and algorithmic penalties:

  • Memory Thrashing ($\mathcal{O}(N)$ Space Complexity): Duplicating a large hash table for hundreds of branches triggers frequent systemic heap allocations, saturating memory pools and blowing up cache lines.
  • Lack of Dynamic Reflection: Cloned maps act as dead snapshots. If a root context receives a late global definition, existing child branches cannot see it unless a costly and complex manual synchronization protocol is implemented.
  • Destruction of Cache Locality: Independent clones distribute elements across disparate virtual memory addresses, confusing the hardware prefetcher and inducing relentless cache missing (pointer chasing).

To solve this, the yaucl library (logds::yaucl::gamma_context) implements a zero-overhead, single-threaded Persistent LinkedHashMap View that transparently provides isolated Copy-on-Write (CoW) semantics with dynamic parent delegation.

3. Industrial Applications Beyond Programming Language Theory

While the structural design of yaucl’s gamma_context directly mimics the behavior of a typing environment (\Gamma), the core engineering challenges it addresses—handling millions of isolated, multi-topology sub-contexts derived from a massive root snapshot while minimizing memory allocations—are prevalent across several massive-scale engineering domains.

Any system driven by state-space exploration, combinatorial optimization, or real-time spatial tracking encounters identical performance walls when utilizing standard data replication. By decoupling topology management through an Arena Memory Pool, the following industrial domains can bypass the (\mathcal{O}(N)) cloning bottleneck.

I. Constraint Programming & SAT Solvers

In industrial logistics (e.g., global airline crew scheduling, dynamic vehicle routing, or 5G frequency spectrum allocation), constraint solvers traverse immense combinatorial decision trees using backtracking algorithms like Branch and Bound.

  • The Context Matrix: The root view maps global resources and rigid operational constraints (e.g., labor laws, hardware ceilings).
  • The Branching Penalty: The solver evaluates millions of alternative state configurations per second. Each path appends temporary local constraints and adjusts resource priority queues.
  • The yaucl Advantage: Replicating full constraint matrices across millions of tentative sub-branches induces catastrophic heap saturation. yaucl lets child nodes share the massive root configuration for free, limiting the allocation cost strictly to the local, ammortized branch boundaries.

II. Algorithmic Backtesting & Temporal Financial Series

Quantitative financial platforms execute intensive scenario simulations (stress-testing) against historical market snapshots to evaluate high-frequency trading models.

  • The Context Matrix: A detailed, multi-gigabyte snapshot of asset prices, volumes, and order-book queues at a specific market opening microsecond ($T_0$).
  • The Branching Penalty: The framework forks millions of concurrent timelines (speculative horizons) to simulate market shocks, liquidity drains, or volatility spikes.
  • The yaucl Advantage: Instead of storing multiple independent full-stack snapshots of the order book, the Arena-backed view isolates only the targeted asset shifts. The system maintains a continuous $\mathcal{O}(1)$ query throughput across all speculative timelines while sharing 90% of the historical market data footprint.

III. Dynamic Routing Engines & GIS Databases

Large-scale logistics platforms (e.g., fleet orchestration engines, dynamic delivery network routing) track and guide millions of couriers simultaneously across a shared national road grid.

  • The Context Matrix: The static topology of the national geographic grid containing millions of nodes (intersections) and edges (streets).
  • The Branching Penalty: Every active delivery vehicle evaluates personal routing options affected by temporary, dynamic events (e.g., local traffic accidents, flash weather delays, or shifting drop-off sequences).
  • The yaucl Advantage: By pairing Small Object Optimization (SOO) with block-contiguous layouts, routing searches (such as real-time variants of A* or Dijkstra) navigate the static road infrastructure at raw L1 cache speeds, isolating regional traffic overrides to the precise driver view context without muddying the immutable base graph.

IV. Motion Planning for Autonomous Robotics

Kinodynamic motion planning and real-time collision avoidance in autonomous drones or self-driving vehicles demand predictable, bare-metal low latencies.

  • The Context Matrix: The dense, three-dimensional spatial point cloud captured by LiDAR and radar arrays during the preceding hardware cycle.
  • The Branching Penalty: Predictive control systems (such as Monte Carlo Tree Search) evaluate millions of physical trajectory options over the subsequent 3-second window to bypass sudden obstacles.
  • The yaucl Advantage: In safety-critical embedded environments, runtime garbage collection pauses or unbounded heap allocation latency can lead to mechanical system failure. The single-threaded, lock-free nature of yaucl guarantees deterministic, sub-millisecond execution cycles directly at the CPU register layer.

Summary of State-Space Persistence Across Industries

The matrix below establishes how the single-threaded persistent view architecture systematically transforms execution bottlenecks across divergent industrial domains:

Industrial Domain Root Context (\Gamma) Contents Local CoW Trigger Event Backtracking Traversal Penalty Core Arena Pool Optimization
SAT & Constraint Solvers Rigid global resources and problem boundary states Local resource assignment / temporary constraint injection Extreme. Millions of branches pruned and discarded per second. Eliminates unamortized heap allocation during deep recursive search sweeps.
Quantitative Finance Immutable asset and order-book historical market snapshots Speculative price variations or macro market shocks Medium. Segmented for isolated parallel stress-test simulations. Shares up to 95% of static time-series baselines across all active horizons.
GIS & Fleet Logistics Static national road grid graph infrastructure Real-time local traffic delays / courier delivery sequence updates Low. Bound to individual courier trip lifecycle steps. Navigates unchanged graph networks at high-density hardware cache speeds.
Autonomous Robotics Raw LiDAR sensor environment point cloud maps Dynamic geometric escape trajectory simulations High. Complete tree sets discarded and recalculated every 100 ms. Zero-latency assurance. Bypasses garbage collection micro-stalls entirely.

3. Architectural Desiderata

To realize an optimal persistent context structure, five architectural pillars were strictly formalized in the design of yaucl:

  1. Shared Multi-Topology Nodes: A single concrete value node must be capable of simultaneously existing across multiple independent lists/views without data replication.
  2. Decoupled View-Specific Inverted Index: Value nodes must maintain isolated next and prev routing tables indexed by a precise view identifier (ListId). This ensures that changing the topological position of a node in a child view leaves its routing in the parent view completely untouched.
  3. Lazy Delegation & Structural Extension: A child view must be instantiated in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time and space. Lookups recursively bubble up to the parent view unless the targeted key has been locally overridden.
  4. Constant-Time Associative Lookup: The collection must provide strict $\mathcal{O}(1)$ key-to-node access, behaving like a synchronized LinkedHashMap for all internal states.
  5. Axiom of Mutation-by-Reappend: Modifying the value associated with an existing key is logically equivalent to structurally evicting that specific node from the view’s current sequence and appending a new node at the tail with the updated payload. This ensures the structural linearity required by dependent type systems.

4. Architectural Deep-Dive: Implementation Layout in Yaucl

To achieve bare-metal performance while honoring the algebraic constraints of $\Gamma$, the implementation in the yaucl open-source library completely avoids dynamic dispatch, type-tag wrappers, and virtual tables. Instead, it relies on a flat, header-only, cache-aligned layout divided into five decoupled components.

The UML-like physical pipeline operates as a unified entity:

       [ ViewFactory ]  <--- (Manages Chunked Memory & GC)
              |
              | allocate_node()
              v
 [ HierarchicalListView ] <===> [ MultiNodeV2 ] <---> [ Independent Lists ]
   (Flat / Lazy State)          (Inverted Index)       (Parent/Sibling Views)

I. Multi-Topology Inverted Indexing (MultiNode.h)

The structural core is defined in MultiNode.h. Traditional nodes in a doubly-linked list store exactly two pointers: next and prev. To allow a node to co-exist in an arbitrary number of sub-contexts and backtracking branches simultaneously, MultiNodeV2 internalizes an Inverted Index Map indexed by a unique ListId:

template <typename Key, typename Value>
struct MultiNodeV2 {
    Key key;
    Value value;
    
    // Inverted index for cross-view multi-topology navigation
    std::unordered_map<ListId, MultiNodeV2*> next;
    std::unordered_map<ListId, MultiNodeV2*> prev;
    
    void set_links(ListId id, MultiNodeV2* p, MultiNodeV2* n);
};

To optimize the Principle of Locality for typical scoping patterns where only a few views concurrently contain a specific hot-spot node, the library can utilize Small Object Optimization (SOO): storing the first (K) list links inside an inline, static stack array to avoid hitting the node’s local hash map unless branching limits are exceeded.

II. The Zero-Cost Arena Pool Allocator (ViewFactory.h)

Allocating nodes sparsely across the heap via standard new or std::make_shared invalidates cache locality and adds substantial metadata tracking overhead. ViewFactory.h acts as an Arena Allocator / Memory Pool that handles memory contiguity:

template <typename Key, typename Value>
class ViewFactory {
private:
    static constexpr std::size_t BLOCK_SIZE = 4096;
    struct ArenaBlock {
        MultiNodeV2<Key, Value> storage[BLOCK_SIZE];
        std::size_t used = 0;
    };
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<ArenaBlock>> arena;
public:
    template <typename... Args>
    MultiNodeV2<Key, Value>* allocate_node(Args&&... args);
};
  • Bump Allocation: Requesting a node reduces to a pointer increment (used++) inside the current active ArenaBlock, executing in strict (\mathcal{O}(1)) time (typically 1 CPU clock cycle).
  • Deferred Link Garbage Collection: When a short-lived backtracking view dies, searching and scrubbing its references across all nodes would cost an expensive (\mathcal{O}(N)) scan. ViewFactory implements deferred reclamation: old ListId routing slots are left stale inside the nodes. Since the underlying memory is owned entirely by the ViewFactory blocks, the entire tree of contexts is safely reclaimed in a single, bulk deallocation pass when the factory scope terminates.

III. Dual-State Monolithic Abstraction (HierarchicalListView.h)

Rather than relying on runtime polymorphism—which destroys compiler loop unrolling and inlining passes due to virtual table lookups—HierarchicalListView.h encapsulates both the Pure Flat State and the Lazy Hierarchical State inside a single concrete class:

template<typename Key, typename Value>
class HierarchicalListView {
private:
    bool is_pure_flat_mode = false;
    
    // Flat State backing structures (Active when N <= 2000)
    std::list<std::pair<Key, Value>> flat_list;
    std::unordered_map<Key, typename std::list<std::pair<Key, Value>>::iterator> flat_lookup;

    // Lazy State backing structures (Active when N > 2000)
    std::unordered_map<Key, MultiNodeV2<Key, Value>*> local_lookup;
    HierarchicalListView* parent = nullptr;
};

The data structure uses its current size at birth to alter its mechanical routing layout transparently:

  • Micro-Scale Birth Activation: If a child view is spawned and the parent’s size is under the 2,000-node threshold, is_pure_flat_mode is set to true. The view completely severs the parent pointer (parent = nullptr) and performs a high-speed L1-cache contiguous clone of the elements into its local standard layout. Lookups and updates bypass all delegation checking.
  • Macro-Scale Lazy Activation: Beyond 2,000 nodes, the view activates its hierarchical structures, referencing the parent pointer. It delegates lookups upward and intercepts modifications through its localized, ammortized telemetry. If local mutations hit the 20% spatial threshold, the internal detach() loop drains the parent chain, fetches the nodes from the contiguous ViewFactory arena, and seamlessly flattens the local topology without shifting the public API context of the type-checker.

5. Ammortized Time and Space Complexity Analysis

To calculate the exact breakeven threshold without empirical approximations, we must formalize and contrast the cost equations of the Lazy Hierarchical State versus the Deferred Global Detach.

Let us assume a parent context Γ containing N total nodes. The child view executes M write operations (update_value / move_to_tail) and R read operations (find_node / iteration). We define the modification ratio as $\alpha = \frac{M}{N}$ (where $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$).

I. CPU Time Cost Modeling

We define the elementary hardware/software costs expressed in execution CPU cycles:

  • $C_{hash}$: Cost of computing the hash and performing a lookup in an std::unordered_map.
  • $C_{arena}$: Cost of a single $\mathcal{O}(1)$ bump allocation inside the pre-allocated contiguous Arena Pool ($C_{arena} \ll C_{alloc_heap}$).
  • $C_{gree}$: Cost of a raw pointer assignment (close to zero, ≈ 1 CPU cycle).

Case A: Remaining in Lazy Hierarchical Mode for all M mutations

Each sparse write triggers a granular Copy-on-Write adjustment. The total cost for R reads and M writes is:

\[T_{lazy} = M \cdot \left( C_{hash} + C_{arena} \right) + R \cdot C_{hash}\]
  • Asymptotic Time Complexity: $\mathcal{O}(M + R)$. Because there are no cross-view locks, lookups and telemetry increments run at native single-thread register speed.

Case B: Triggering a Global detach()

The view clones all unmutated elements from the parent to achieve full independence, storing them sequentially. Subsequent M writes and R reads execute directly on clean, local raw pointers.

\[T_{detach} = \underbrace{N \cdot \left( C_{arena} + C_{hash} \right)}_{\text{Fixed Detach Cost}} + M \cdot C_{gree} + R \cdot C_{gree}\]
  • Asymptotic Time Complexity: $\mathcal{O}(N + M + R)$.

Resolution of the Temporal Breakeven Point

Equating the two costs ($T_{lazy} = T_{detach}$) and isolating the threshold ratio $\alpha = \frac{M}{N}$, we find that a global detach becomes computationally superior when:

\[\alpha > \frac{1}{1 + \frac{C_{hash}}{C_{arena}}} - \frac{R}{N} \cdot \left( \frac{C_{hash} - C_{gree}}{C_{hash} + C_{arena}} \right)\]

Substituting the cycles of a modern single-threaded architecture under Clang -O3 ($C_{arena} \approx 5$, $C_{hash} \approx 15$, $C_{gree} \approx 1$): \(\alpha > 0.75 - 0.70 \cdot \left(\frac{R}{N}\right)\)

  • Low Read Intensity (R → 0): The temporal threshold rises toward $\alpha \to 0.75$. It is highly efficient to remain in the lazy hierarchical state until nearly 75% of the context has been mutated.
  • High Read Intensity (R ≈ N): Frequent traversals lower the temporal breakeven point down to $\alpha \approxeq 0.05$ (5%), as direct raw pointer evaluation quickly amortizes the fixed cloning cost.

II. RAM Space Cost Modeling

We analyze memory allocation in bytes on a 64-bit architecture:

  • A raw pointer occupies 8 bytes.
  • An isolated node after a structural detach occupies: $\text{Dim}_{\text{node}} = \text{Key} + \text{Value} + 16 \text{ bytes}$ (two raw routing pointers).
  • An internal index map within the node or view under partial load occupies a fixed metadata base of $\approx 48$ bytes plus bucket overhead. We quantify the cumulative indexing footprint as $\text{Overhead}_{\text{hash}} \approx 256 \text{ bytes}$ per node due to distributed bucket layouts.

Case A: Memory in Lazy Hierarchical State

The child view allocates memory only for the $M$ mutated nodes, but those nodes must store their view-specific inverted indexes inside their internal maps: \(S_{lazy} = M \cdot \left( \text{Dim}_{\text{node}} + \text{Overhead}_{\text{hash}} \right)\)

Case B: Memory in Standalone Flat State (Post-Detach)

The view duplicates all $N$ nodes, but since they are structurally isolated, they drop the inverted index tracking for the child view, routing via contiguous raw pointers: \(S_{flat} = N \cdot \text{Dim}_{\text{node}}\)

Resolution of the Spatial Breakeven Point

Setting $S_{lazy} = S_{flat}$: \(M \cdot \left( \text{Dim}_{\text{node}} + \text{Overhead}_{\text{hash}} \right) = N \cdot \text{Dim}_{\text{node}}\) \(\alpha_{memory} = \frac{\text{Dim}_{\text{node}}}{\text{Dim}_{\text{node}} + \text{Overhead}_{\text{hash}}}\)

For standard compiler token primitives (Key = std::string, Value = std::string), $\text{Dim}_{\text{node}} \approx 64 \text{ bytes}$: \(\alpha_{memory} = \frac{64}{64 + 256} = \frac{64}{320} = 0.20 \implies \mathbf{20\%}\)

Rigorous Analytical Conclusion

The mathematical intersection proves that the optimal state transition is governed by two constraints in the $(\alpha, R/N)$ space:

Modification Ratio (α)
  100% |-----------------------------------------------------------------------
       |                                                                      /
       |                     CPU TIME BENEFIT ZONE                           / 
       |       (Saves cloning cycles, but increases RAM overhead)            /  
   75% |-------------------------------------------------------------------/ <- Temporal Limit (If R -> 0)
       |                                                                 / 
       |                                                                /  
       |                                                               /   
   20% |--------------------------------------------------------------/ <- Rigid Memory Bound (Hash Oversize)
       |                                                            /
       |             ABSOLUTE BENEFIT ZONE (TIME & RAM)            / <- CPU Breakeven Line (As R/N increases)
    0% |----------------------------------------------------------/------------
       0                                                        1             2   Read / Total Nodes Ratio (R/N)
       [ Low Read Intensity / Fast Backtracking ]            [ High Read Intensity / Massive Reductions ]
  1. Rigid Memory Constraint (Y-Axis): Regardless of read frequency, once local modifications exceed 20% ($\alpha = 0.20$), the memory overhead of the node inverted indexes surpasses the cost of cloning the entire context down into a flat sequence.
  2. Flexible Time Constraint (X-Axis): In heavy read-intensive scenarios ($\frac{R}{N} \ge 1$), the micro-delays of parent chain delegation make an immediate flat layout superior at lower mutation rates, while a single-threaded execution with minimal lookups stretches the lazy threshold up to 75%.

6. Discussion of Empirical Benchmarking Results

The architecture was evaluated under single-threaded conditions, compiled with Clang 15 -O3 on an Intel® Core™ Ultra 9 185H × 22, simulating a type-checker processing a global scope ($\Gamma$) with 50 parallel backtracking evaluation branches.

The Micro-Scale Penalty ($10 \le N \le 1000$)

At highly localized dimensions, the native flat map clone wins, operating around 0.42x – 0.62x the speed of our view. This represents an explicit hardware reality: a map holding fewer than 1,000 elements can be duplicated inside a single L1/L2 cache line swap. On this micro-scale, the pointer dereferencing and logical branching (if (parent)) of our persistent view introduce subtle pipeline bubble delays. However, in absolute terms, the difference is negligible (less than 11 milliseconds across an entire evaluation tree).

The Macro-Scale Break-Even ($N = 10,000$)

At ten thousand active keys, the overhead of re-hashing and heap-allocating full containers under standard STL starts to match the delegation steps of the view. The structures perform at a statistical tie (0.88x).

The Domain of Asymptotic Dominance ($N \ge 100,000$)

As $N$ scales into production compiler environments, the standard replication model collapses under memory allocation thrashing.

  • At 1,000,000 elements, standard replication requires a painful 35.59 seconds due to widespread heap fragmentation. The yaucl structure resolves the exact same evaluation sequence in a mere 1.58 seconds (a 22.41x speedup).
  • At 10,000,000 elements, the gap expands dramatically: standard replication stalls the CPU for over 8.8 minutes (528,200 ms), while the optimized Arena-backed view completes in 16.25 seconds, delivering an unyielding 32.50x performance multiplication.

By eliminating pointer chasing through block-contiguous memory layouts and dynamically managing context isolation, yaucl successfully implements an immutable functional concept at the raw speed of bare-metal imperative design.

Macro Scale (N > 2000, α ≤ 20%) 🟢 Lazy Hierarchical Bump Allocation inside the contiguous Arena Pool. Zero-cost node sharing. Zero dynamic heap allocations. Asymptotic Dominance ($5.76x$ up to $32.50x$ performance gain).

entry.title: Deep-Dive Tutorial: Programmatic Control Flow (`prim::If` & `prim::Loop`) in LibTorch JIT C++

link.title: Deep-Dive Tutorial: Programmatic Control Flow (`prim::If` & `prim::Loop`) in LibTorch JIT C++

entry.content:
When building modular execution frameworks using PyTorch’s native C++ API (LibTorch), developers often need to construct computational graphs without relying on string-based Python compilation frontends. This requires manually orchestrating the lower-level Intermediate Representation (IR) using the programmatic torch::jit::Graph API.

While linear pipelines are straightforward, injecting structured control flow blocks—specifically prim::If and prim::Loop—presents stringent architectural constraints. A single type misalignment or a single parameter index drift will crash LibTorch’s underlying execution engine or corrupt your serialized .pt binary models.

This tutorial breaks down the technical definitions of structured control flow directly from the PyTorch JIT architecture documentation, translates them into exact C++ implementations, and analyzes the low-level prerequisites required to achieve stable code execution.

1. Core Architectural Definitions

Unlike unstructured compilers that use control-flow graphs (CFGs) with explicit jump statements or branch blocks, PyTorch JIT uses Structured Control Flow implemented via sub-Block hierarchies. This structural enforcement simplifies optimization passes (like constant propagation and shape refinement) and guarantees clear Single-Static Assignment (SSA) form dependencies.

A. The If-Statement (prim::If)

From the documentation, a conditional block is modeled as follows:

  • No Block Inputs: The Block boundaries of an if-statement (block0 for true, block1 for false) do not accept entry inputs or parameter arguments.
  • Block Outputs as Φ (Phi) Channels: Values modified across both code tracks must be declared as block outputs via registerOutput().
  • Symmetric Output Matching: Both branches must return the exact same number of outputs in the exact same type sequence. The containing prim::If node then mirrors these internal registers out to the parent graph block (addOutput()), performing a role similar to an SSA Φ function.
%y_1, ..., %y_r = prim::If(%condition)
  block0():  # TRUE BRANCH -> Returns r outputs
    ...
    -> (%t_1, ..., %t_r)
  block1():  # FALSE BRANCH -> Returns r outputs
    ...
    -> (%f_1, ..., %f_r)

B. The Loop-Statement (prim::Loop)

The prim::Loop node handles both while and for loop abstractions with a unified semantic schema. It relies heavily on Loop-Carried Dependencies:

%y_1, ..., %y_r = prim::Loop(%max_trip_count, %initial_condition, %x_1, ..., %x_r)
  block0(%i, %a_1, ..., %a_r):
    ...
    -> (%iter_condition, %b_1, ..., %b_r)

The sequence demands strict layout symmetry across four operational points:

  1. Loop Node Inputs: Receives %max_trip_count (the integer execution ceiling), %initial_condition (the entry boolean), and the initial values for all state dependencies (%x_1, ..., %x_r).
  2. Block Parameter Inputs: loop_block->addInput() expects the JIT loop iteration index (%i) as its absolute first argument (Index 0). The following entries map directly to the active loop-carried variables (%a_1, ..., %a_r).
  3. Block Termination Outputs: At the end of the block, registerOutput() requires the trailing continuation condition (%iter_condition) at Index 0. Passing a constant false here immediately signals an early loop termination (break). This is followed by the mutated values to carry into the next cycle (%b_1, ..., %b_r).
  4. Loop Node Outputs: The external loop_node->addOutput() tracking channels must explicitly match the quantity and types of the internal carried state values (%y_1, ..., %y_r), skipping the loop tracking parameters.

2. Low-Level Requirements to Ensure Code Stability

To build these subgraphs programmatically without crashing PyTorch’s ScriptModuleSerializer or throwing evaluation exceptions, you must satisfy three low-level requirements:

I. Operator Overload Signatures: Tensors vs. Scalars

PyTorch IR relies on strict function overloading. For example, aten::add has completely different argument counts depending on the input types:

  • Tensor Addition: Requires 3 arguments: (Tensor self, Tensor other, Scalar alpha).
  • Primitive Scalar Addition: Requires exactly 2 arguments: (int self, int other) -> int.

When manipulating loop counters or scalar variables, passing a third argument like alpha to a purely scalar addition breaks schema validation and corrupts the execution trace.

// CORRECT: Primitive scalar addition for loop counters (2 arguments)
torch::jit::Node* next_counter = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::add, {counter_curr, const_1});

II. Output Layer Purging via eraseOutput

When creating high-level conditional nodes like prim::If or prim::Loop using graph->create, LibTorch may automatically assign implicit fallback slots or track floating output nodes in memory. When explicitly designing structured Φ registers or type definitions, you must clear out accidental background slots using a cleanup loop before running your type configuration:

while (if_node->outputs().size() > 0) {
    if_node->eraseOutput(0);
}

Failing to purge these channels leads to asymmetries and causes the Python printer to output extra ghost variables (like _10 or _24), crashing your code reload step.

III. Explicit Class Allocation for Serializer Contexts

If a graph is intended to be exported and saved to a file via module.save(), any custom data configurations like TupleType structures can be created anonymously. The ScriptModuleSerializer traverses the complete compilation database to construct clean Python environment representations.

auto tuple_return_type = c10::TupleType::create({int_type, tensor_type});
cu->register_type(tuple_return_type); // CRITICAL: Makes the type discoverable by the serializer

C++ LibTorch JIT

I now showcase the code required to generate the Python code stated above:

#include <torch/script.h>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <memory>
#include <limits>

int main(void) {
auto cu = std::make_shared<torch::jit::CompilationUnit>();
    auto class_name = c10::QualifiedName("__torch__.ConditionalLoopModule");
    auto class_type = c10::ClassType::create(class_name, cu, /*is_module=*/true);
    torch::jit::Module module_(cu, class_type);

    auto graph = std::make_shared<torch::jit::Graph>();

    // 1. Module input for the forward function, represented as a dataflow graph
    torch::jit::Value* self_val = graph->addInput("self")->setType(class_type);
    torch::jit::Value* input_val = graph->addInput("input_val")->setType(c10::TensorType::get());

    // =========================================================================
    // 2. Main constants 
    // =========================================================================
    torch::jit::Value* const_max_int = graph->insertConstant(std::numeric_limits<int64_t>::max())->setType(c10::IntType::get()); // %80
    torch::jit::Value* const_true    = graph->insertConstant(true)->setType(c10::BoolType::get());                     // %8
    torch::jit::Value* status_init   = graph->insertConstant((int64_t)0)->setType(c10::IntType::get());                // %status.1
    torch::jit::Value* const_2       = graph->insertConstant((int64_t)2)->setType(c10::IntType::get());                // %3
    torch::jit::Value* const_20      = graph->insertConstant((int64_t)20)->setType(c10::IntType::get());               // %5
    torch::jit::Value* const_1       = graph->insertConstant((int64_t)1)->setType(c10::IntType::get());                // %22
    torch::jit::Value* loop_counter_init = graph->insertConstant((int64_t)0)->setType(c10::IntType::get());            // Contatore iniziale range(20)
    torch::jit::Value* const_false   = graph->insertConstant(false)->setType(c10::BoolType::get());                   // %55

    // Some float constants
    torch::jit::Value* const_0_05    = graph->insertConstant(0.05)->setType(c10::FloatType::get());                    // %13
    torch::jit::Value* const_0_01    = graph->insertConstant(0.01)->setType(c10::FloatType::get());                    // %17
    torch::jit::Value* const_10      = graph->insertConstant(10.0)->setType(c10::FloatType::get());                    // %25

    // 3. Initial computation, outside the loop value = input_val * 2
    torch::jit::Node* mul_node = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::mul, {input_val, const_2});
    graph->insertNode(mul_node);
    torch::jit::Value* value_init = mul_node->output()->setType(c10::TensorType::get());

    // =========================================================================
    // 4. CREAZIONE DEL NODO PRIM::LOOP
    // So to slavishly follow PyTorch JIT requirements:
    // input order: max_trip, cond_in, status_init, value_init, counter_init (status_init is reused as counter within the target graph)
    // =========================================================================
    torch::jit::Node* loop_node = graph->create(torch::jit::prim::Loop, {const_max_int, const_true, status_init, value_init, status_init});
    graph->insertNode(loop_node);

    torch::jit::Block* loop_block = loop_node->addBlock();

    // Input of the native IR block
    loop_block->addInput()->setType(c10::IntType::get()); // Implicit JIT Iterator
    torch::jit::Value* status_curr = loop_block->addInput()->setType(c10::IntType::get());   // Int
    torch::jit::Value* value_curr  = loop_block->addInput()->setType(c10::TensorType::get());  // Tensor
    torch::jit::Value* counter_curr = loop_block->addInput()->setType(c10::IntType::get()); // Int (the counter

    // --- Some Internal Loop Logic ---
    // value = value * (i+1) * 0.05
    // Incrementing the counter for the for loop
    torch::jit::Node* next_counter = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::add, {counter_curr, const_1});
    loop_block->appendNode(next_counter);
    torch::jit::Value* counter = next_counter->output()->setType(c10::IntType::get());
    torch::jit::Node* mul_i = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::mul, {value_curr, counter});
    loop_block->appendNode(mul_i);
    torch::jit::Node* mul_0_05 = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::mul, {mul_i->output(), const_0_05});
    loop_block->appendNode(mul_0_05);
    torch::jit::Value* value_scaled = mul_0_05->output()->setType(c10::TensorType::get());

    // Condition: torch::all(value > 0.01)
    torch::jit::Node* gt_node = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::gt, {value_scaled, const_0_01});
    loop_block->appendNode(gt_node);
    torch::jit::Node* all_node = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::all, {gt_node->output()});
    loop_block->appendNode(all_node);
    torch::jit::Node* bool_cast = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::Bool, {all_node->output()});
    loop_block->appendNode(bool_cast);
    torch::jit::Value* if_condition = bool_cast->output()->setType(c10::BoolType::get());

    // =========================================================================
    // 5. CREATING THE CONDITIONAL PRIM::IF WITHIN THE LOOP
    // =========================================================================
    torch::jit::Node* if_node = graph->create(torch::jit::prim::If, {if_condition});
    loop_block->appendNode(if_node);

    torch::jit::Block* then_block = if_node->addBlock();
    torch::jit::Block* else_block = if_node->addBlock();

    //  THEN (True) branch -> output: (continue, status, value)
    torch::jit::Node* then_add = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::add, {value_scaled, const_10, const_1});
    then_block->appendNode(then_add);
    torch::jit::Value* result = then_add->output()->setType(c10::TensorType::get());

    then_block->registerOutput(const_true);
    then_block->registerOutput(const_1);
    then_block->registerOutput(result);

    //  ELSE (False / BREAK) branch -> output: (continue, status, value)
    else_block->registerOutput(const_false);
    else_block->registerOutput(status_curr);
    else_block->registerOutput(value_scaled);

    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // CRITICAL FIX: Clearing and forcing the final 3 outputs over nodo prim::If
    // This ensures to completely remove a host fourth registry (_10) from our final Python code!
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    while (if_node->outputs().size() > 0) {
        if_node->eraseOutput(0);
    }

    torch::jit::Value* if_continue = if_node->addOutput()->setType(c10::BoolType::get());
    torch::jit::Value* if_status   = if_node->addOutput()->setType(c10::IntType::get());
    torch::jit::Value* if_value    = if_node->addOutput()->setType(c10::TensorType::get());
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------


    // Check maximum bounded loop iterations: counter < 20
    // Simulating the for loop with a while-condition over the cycle upper bound
    torch::jit::Node* lt_node = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::lt, {counter, const_20});
    loop_block->appendNode(lt_node);
    torch::jit::Value* ltout = lt_node->output()->setType(c10::BoolType::get());

    // Total stopping condition: (counter < 20) AND (if_continue)
    torch::jit::Node* and_node = graph->create(torch::jit::aten::__and__, {ltout, if_continue});
    loop_block->appendNode(and_node);
    torch::jit::Value* loop_keep_going = and_node->output()->setType(c10::BoolType::get());


    // =========================================================================
    // 6. Setting the total output registries
    // Index 0: Continuation gate signal (loop_keep_going)
    // Index 1+: Loops back modified current tracking states (status, value, counter)
    // =========================================================================
    loop_block->registerOutput(loop_keep_going);
    loop_block->registerOutput(if_status);
    loop_block->registerOutput(if_value);
    loop_block->registerOutput(counter);

    // =========================================================================
    // 7. Setting outer block's results
    // Clean, trace, and align external return values with inner dependencies 1:1
    // =========================================================================
    while (loop_node->outputs().size() > 0) {
        loop_node->eraseOutput(0);
    }
    torch::jit::Value* final_status  = loop_node->addOutput()->setType(c10::IntType::get());
    torch::jit::Value* final_value   = loop_node->addOutput()->setType(c10::TensorType::get());
    torch::jit::Value* final_counter = loop_node->addOutput()->setType(c10::IntType::get());

    // =========================================================================
    // 8. Returning multiple values as elements of a tuple
    // Pack only final_status and final_value, dropping the trailing loop counter variable
    // =========================================================================
    torch::jit::Node* tuple_node = graph->create(torch::jit::prim::TupleConstruct, {final_status, final_value});
    graph->insertNode(tuple_node);
    graph->registerOutput(tuple_node->output());

    auto tensor_type = c10::TensorType::get();
    auto int_type = c10::IntType::get();
    auto tuple_name = c10::QualifiedName("__torch__.MyReturnTypeTuple");
    auto tuple_return_type = c10::TupleType::create({int_type, tensor_type});
    cu->register_type(tuple_return_type);
    tuple_node->output()->setType(tuple_return_type);

    // =========================================================================
    // 9. Final schema compilation
    // =========================================================================
    std::vector<c10::Argument> arguments = {
        c10::Argument("self", class_type),
        c10::Argument("input_val", tensor_type)
    };
    std::vector<c10::Argument> returns = {
        c10::Argument("", tuple_return_type)
    };

    c10::QualifiedName method_name(class_name, "forward");
    c10::FunctionSchema schema(method_name.name(), "", arguments, returns);

    auto method = module_._ivalue()->compilation_unit()->create_function(method_name, graph);
    method->setSchema(std::move(schema));
    class_type->addMethod(method);

    module_.save("conditional_subgraph.pt");
    std::cout << "Modello salvato." << std::endl;

    return 0;
    }

Python driver

The following execution script handles loading your generated graph, executes a step-by-step mathematical state validation tracer, and inspects the structural text layout.

import torch


def simulate_evolution(input_val, max_cycles=20):
    """
    Simula esattamente il comportamento del grafo JIT C++ ciclo per ciclo
    per mostrare l'evoluzione delle variabili e calcolare il risultato atteso.
    """
    print("\n--- Pure Python simulation of the expected behaviour of our JIT code ---")
    status = 0
    # outer computation value = input_val * 2
    value = input_val.clone() * 2
    print(f"Initial configuration -> status: {status}, value:\n{value}")

    for i in range(max_cycles):
        # 1. Multiplication per the next iteration index
        value_scaled = value * (i+1) * 0.05

        # 2. Checking the condition over the scaled value
        condition = torch.all(value_scaled > 0.01).item()

        print(f"\n[Iteration #{i:02d}] -> Times i={i} and 0.05")
        print(f"         -> After multiplication:\n{value_scaled}")
        print(f"         -> Check (value > 0.01)? {condition}")

        if condition:
            status = 1
            value = value_scaled + 10.0
            print(f"         -> [THEN BRANCH] UPDATE! status: {status}, value (con +10):\n{value}")
        else:
            print(f"         -> [ELSE BRANCH] !!! BREAK TRIGGERED !!! We stop here.")
            # Al break, il valore finale che sopravvive è value_scaled (come da blocco else_block in C++)
            value = value_scaled
            break

    return status, value


def test_model_with_evolution(model_path="conditional_subgraph.pt"):
    print(f"--- Loading the JIT model from: {model_path} ---")
    try:
        model = torch.jit.load(model_path)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error while loading the .pt file: {e}")
        return

    # Pick an input that is not going to zero
    input_tensor = torch.ones(2, 2) * 5.0

    # 1. Performing the Python code simulation
    expected_status, expected_value = simulate_evolution(input_tensor, max_cycles=20)

    # 2. Running the JIT-compiled code
    print("\n--- JIT running ---")
    jit_status, jit_value = model(input_tensor)

    print(f"\n=== Checking the final results ===")
    print(f" JIT Status: {jit_status} | Expected status: {expected_status}")
    print(f" JIT Value:\n{jit_value}")
    print(f"Expected outcome:\n{expected_value}")

    # Controllo di uguaglianza formale
    outputs_match = torch.equal(jit_value, expected_value) and (jit_status == expected_status)
    print(f"\nWas the computation correct? {'SÌ ✅' if outputs_match else 'NO ❌'}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_model_with_evolution()

By systematically purging intermediate nodes using eraseOutput and maintaining proper scalar signature definitions, your low-level LibTorch components will translate flawlessly back into cross-compatible Python execution contexts.

entry.title: Expressing Tensorflow 2.x operations in plain Mathematical Notation

link.title: Expressing Tensorflow 2.x operations in plain Mathematical Notation

entry.content:
Despite the vast documentation on Tensorflow operations, those are little to no documented in mathematical notation. This makes it hard to abstract and generalize some of those ideas, as well as make it rather impossible to make those operations accessible for the common mathematician. Here is a little subset of these operations documented in such a fashion. Furthermore, I also note how you can actually use Tensor Algebra to express theta-join operations. You can find a full list of Tensorflow operations here.

1. Element-wise Transformations

These operations apply a scalar function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ independently to each component of a tensor without changing its dimensions.

Mathematical Definition

Given an $N$-order tensor $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{I_1 \times I_2 \times \dots \times I_N}$, the transformation $\mathcal{Y} = f(\mathcal{X})$ is defined component-wise as:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_N} = f\left(\mathcal{X}_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_N}\right)\]

where $i_k \in {1, 2, \dots, I_k}$ for each mode $k$.

TensorFlow Implementation

import tensorflow as tf

# Example using a sigmoid activation function
Y = tf.math.sigmoid(X)

2. Tensor Contractions & Matrix Multiplications

These operations compute inner products over specified matching dimensions, effectively reducing the rank of the combined structures.

Mathematical Definition

General Tensor Contraction

If we contract an order-$P$ tensor $\mathcal{A}$ and an order-$Q$ tensor $\mathcal{B}$ over their last $k$ and first $k$ axes respectively, using Einstein summation convention (implicit summation over repeated indices):

\[\mathcal{C}_{i_1 \dots i_{P-k} j_{k+1} \dots j_Q} = \mathcal{A}_{i_1 \dots i_{P-k} m_1 \dots m_k} \mathcal{B}^{m_1 \dots m_k}_{\phantom{m_1 \dots m_k} j_{k+1} \dots j_Q}\]

Batch Matrix Multiplication

For two 3D tensors representing batches of matrices, $\mathcal{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times I \times J}$ and $\mathcal{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times J \times K}$:

\[\mathcal{C}_{b i k} = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \mathcal{A}_{b i j} \mathcal{B}_{b j k} \implies \mathcal{C}_{b i k} = \mathcal{A}_{b i j} \mathcal{B}_{b \phantom{j} k}^{\phantom{b} j}\]

TensorFlow Implementation

# General Contraction (contracting over last 2 axes of A and first 2 axes of B)
C_dot = tf.tensordot(A, B, axes=2)

# Batch Matrix Multiplication
C_matmul = tf.linalg.matmul(A, B)

3. Axis Permutations and Transpositions

These transformations map tensor coordinates via a permutation function $\pi$, rearranging the axes layout.

Mathematical Definition

Given $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{I_1 \times I_2 \times \dots \times I_N}$ and a bijection $\pi$ of the set of indices ${1, 2, \dots, N}$, the transformed tensor $\mathcal{Y} = \text{permute}(\mathcal{X}, \pi)$ is defined by:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{i_{\pi(1)} i_{\pi(2)} \dots i_{\pi(N)}} = \mathcal{X}_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_N}\]

TensorFlow Implementation

# Permuting axes mapping index positions [0, 1, 2] -> [2, 0, 1]
Y = tf.transpose(X, perm=[2, 0, 1])

4. Tensor Reductions

Reduction transformations collapse specific dimensions by aggregating elements via a binary operator $\bigoplus$ (such as $\sum, \max, \prod$).

Mathematical Definition

If reducing $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{I_1 \times I_2 \times I_3}$ along the second axis ($I_2$) using summation:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{i_1 i_3} = \sum_{i_2=1}^{I_2} \mathcal{X}_{i_1 i_2 i_3} = \mathcal{X}_{i_1 i_2 i_3} \mathbf{1}^{i_2}\]

TensorFlow Implementation

# Reduction along axis 1
Y = tf.reduce_sum(X, axis=1)

5. Linear Convolution Transforms

Spatial transforms that slide a localized kernel filter tensor across a multi-dimensional data tensor.

Mathematical Definition

For a 4D input $\mathcal{X}$ (Batch $b$, Height $h$, Width $w$, Channels $c$) and a filter kernel $\mathcal{K}$ (Filter Height $k_h$, Filter Width $k_w$, Input Channels $c$, Output Filters $f$), with strides $S_h, S_w$:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{b, \, h, \, w, \, f} = \sum_{\delta h} \sum_{\delta w} \sum_{c} \mathcal{X}_{b, \, h \cdot S_h + \delta h, \, w \cdot S_w + \delta w, \, c} \cdot \mathcal{K}_{\delta h, \, \delta w, \, c, \, f}\]

TensorFlow Implementation

Y = tf.nn.conv2d(X, K, strides=[1, 1, 1, 1], padding='SAME')

6. Tensor Slicing

Slicing extracts contiguous sub-tensors by selecting bounded index intervals along target dimensions.

Mathematical Definition

Given $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{I_1 \times I_2 \times \dots \times I_N}$, a slice with starting indices $s_k$, ending indices $e_k$, and steps $t_k$ creates an output $\mathcal{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{J_1 \times J_2 \dots \times J_N}$:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{j_1 j_2 \dots j_N} = \mathcal{X}_{(s_1 + j_1 \cdot t_1)(s_2 + j_2 \cdot t_2)\dots(s_N + j_N \cdot t_N)}\]

where $j_k \in {0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \frac{e_k - s_k - 1}{t_k} \rfloor}$.

TensorFlow Implementation

# Slicing a sub-tensor using standard Python slicing notation
Y = X[s_1:e_1:t_1, s_2:e_2:t_2]

7. Tensor Squeezing

Squeezing eliminates singleton dimensions (axes of size 1) without mutating internal value order.

Mathematical Definition

Let $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{I_1 \times \dots \times I_N}$ where a subset of axes $A$ satisfies $I_a = 1, \forall a \in A$. If $\phi: {1, \dots, M} \to {1, \dots, N} \setminus A$ is a strictly increasing monotonic index mapping:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{j_1 j_2 \dots j_M} = \mathcal{X}_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_N} \quad \text{where } i_k = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k \in A \\ j_{\phi^{-1}(k)} & \text{if } k \notin A \end{cases}\]

TensorFlow Implementation

# Removes all dimensions of size 1
Y = tf.squeeze(X, axis=list(A))

8. Tensor Aggregation

Advanced grouping transformations over segmented regions or cluster mappings.

Mathematical Definition

For a matrix $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J}$ and a segment assignment vector $S \in \mathbb{N}^I$, the segmented aggregation mapping to $\mathcal{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times J}$ evaluates via Kronecker deltas:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{k, j} = \sum_{i=1}^{I} \mathcal{X}_{i, j} \cdot \delta_{k, S_i}\]

TensorFlow Implementation

Y = tf.math.segment_sum(X, segment_ids=S)

9. One-Hot Encoding

Expands a discrete label tensor by adding a categorical indicator axis of depth $D$.

Mathematical Definition

Given $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{N}^{I_1 \times \dots \times I_N}$, active value $\alpha$, and inactive value $\beta$, the expanded encoding $\mathcal{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{I_1 \times \dots \times I_N \times D}$ along target index $d \in {0, \dots, D-1}$ is:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_N d} = \alpha \cdot \delta_{d, \, \mathcal{X}_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_N}} + \beta \cdot \left(1 - \delta_{d, \, \mathcal{X}_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_N}}\right)\]

TensorFlow Implementation

Y = tf.one_hot(X, depth=D, on_value=alpha, off_value=beta)

10. Tensor Gathering and Scattering

Indexed read and write operations mapping sparse index topologies to dense configurations.

Mathematical Definition

Multi-Dimensional Gather (tf.gather_nd)

Extracts indices from source $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{I_0 \dots \times I_{N-1}}$ using coordinate lookup map $\mathcal{R} \in \mathbb{N}^{J_0 \dots \times J_{M-1} \times K}$:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{j_0 \dots j_{M-1} \, i_K \dots i_{N-1}} = \mathcal{X}_{\mathcal{R}_{j_0 \dots j_{M-1} 0}, \, \dots, \, \mathcal{R}_{j_0 \dots j_{M-1} (K-1)}, \, i_K, \, \dots, \, i_{N-1}}\]

Multi-Dimensional Scatter Update (tf.tensor_scatter_nd_add)

Accumulates updates $\mathcal{U}$ into base tensor $\mathcal{X}$ along target indices $\mathcal{R}$:

\[\mathcal{Y}_{i_0 \dots i_{N-1}} = \mathcal{X}_{i_0 \dots i_{N-1}} + \sum_{j_0 \dots j_{M-1}} \mathcal{U}_{j_0 \dots j_{M-1} \, i_K \dots i_{N-1}} \cdot \prod_{k=0}^{K-1} \delta_{i_k, \, \mathcal{R}_{j_0 \dots j_{M-1} k}}\]

TensorFlow Implementation

# Gather multi-dimensional slices
Y_gather = tf.gather_nd(X, R)

# Scatter multi-dimensional updates into an existing tensor
Y_scatter = tf.tensor_scatter_nd_add(X, R, U)

11. Relational $\theta$-Joins Over Tensors

Mimics relational database conditional evaluation across two separate tensors while combining their coordinate spaces.

Mathematical Definition

Given $\mathcal{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{I_1 \times \dots \times I_L}$ with join axis index $\mu$, and $\mathcal{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{J_1 \times \dots \times J_R}$ with join axis index $\nu$:

  1. Broadcast Predicate Matrix Calculation ($\mathcal{M}$): \(\mathcal{M}_{i_1 \dots i_L j_1 \dots j_R} = \mathbb{I}\Big(\mathcal{A}_{i_1 \dots i_mu \dots i_L} \,\, \theta \,\, \mathcal{B}_{j_1 \dots j_\nu \dots j_R}\Big)\)

  2. Coordinate Extraction via Index Lookup Matrix ($\mathcal{R}$): \(\mathcal{R} = \text{positions}(\mathcal{M} == 1) \in \mathbb{N}^{K \times (L+R)}\)

  3. Value Materialization: \(\mathcal{Y}_{k, 0} = \mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{R}_{k, 1}, \dots, \mathcal{R}_{k, L}}, \quad \mathcal{Y}_{k, 1} = \mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{R}_{k, L+1}, \dots, \mathcal{R}_{k, L+R}}\)

TensorFlow Implementation

# Step 1: Reshape to broadcast comparison over targeted axes
# Assumes A is 2D [I, M_axis] and B is 2D [J, N_axis]
A_expanded = tf.expand_dims(tf.expand_dims(A, 1), 2) # Shape: [I, 1, 1, M_axis]
B_expanded = tf.expand_dims(tf.expand_dims(B, 0), 0) # Shape: [1, 1, J, N_axis]

# Compute boolean predicate indicator mask (e.g., theta is strict equality)
M_mask = tf.reduce_all(tf.equal(A_expanded, B_expanded), axis=-1)

# Step 2 & 3: Find valid matching coordinates and materialize entries

R_coords = tf.where(M_mask)
vals_A = tf.gather_nd(A, R_coords[:, :2])
vals_B = tf.gather_nd(B, R_coords[:, 2:])
Y_join = tf.concat([vals_A, vals_B], axis=-1)

12. Complex Contextual Multi-Axis Tensor Expressions

This section demonstrates how to formulate complex, arbitrary multi-axis expressions combining generalized Einstein contractions, cell-wise logical operators ($\vee$), and existential quantifiers (∃) acting over explicit sets of axes.

We formalize the evaluation of a target indicator expression: \(\mathbb{I}(\exists I. \theta(\sum_J M[J;I]))\) where I and J are distinct index tuples (sets of axes) rather than singular dimensions.

Mathematical Definition

Given a tensor $\mathcal{M}$ spanning multi-index layout spaces $\mathbf{j} = (j_1, \dots, j_m) \in J$ and $\mathbf{i} = (i_1, \dots, i_n) \in I$:

  1. Multi-Index Contraction over Set J: \(\mathcal{Z}_{\mathbf{i}} = \sum_{j_1} \dots \sum_{j_m} \mathcal{M}_{(j_1, \dots, j_m, \, i_1, \dots, i_n)}\)

  2. Existential Quantifier Disjunction over Set I via Predicate θ: \(y = \mathbb{I}\left(\exists \mathbf{i} \in I . \, \theta(\mathcal{Z}_{\mathbf{i}})\right) = \bigvee_{i_1} \dots \bigvee_{i_n} \mathbb{I}\big(\theta(\mathcal{Z}_{(i_1, \dots, i_n)})\big)\)

Alternatively, using an algebraic bounding framework without explicit boolean branching logic: \(y = \text{clip}\left( \sum_{i_1} \dots \sum_{i_n} \mathbb{I}\big(\theta(\mathcal{Z}_{\mathbf{i}})\big), \,\, 0, \,\, 1 \right)\)

For cell-wise logical OR ($\vee$) statements matching conditions such as $\mathcal{A}{ijk} > 0 \vee \mathcal{B}{ijk} > 0$, the indicator evaluates as: \(\text{Logical\_OR}(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B}) = \max\Big( \mathbb{I}(\mathcal{A} > 0), \, \mathbb{I}(\mathcal{B} > 0) \Big)\)

TensorFlow Implementation

import tensorflow as tf

# Define numerical axis positions corresponding to index sets J and I
# Example assuming M is a 5D tensor: J maps to axes, I maps to axes [2, 3, 4]
axes_J = [0, 1]
axes_I = [2, 3, 4]

# 1. Compute multi-axis contraction over the designated axis indices in set J
Z = tf.reduce_sum(M, axis=axes_J)

# 2. Evaluate cell-wise condition theta (e.g., matching a numerical boundary)
# Includes element-wise logical OR implementation logic example via '|'
condition_mask = (Z > 0.0) | (Z < -1.0)

# 3. Handle Existential Quantifier ($\exists$ I) collapsing multi-axis set I
exists_condition = tf.reduce_any(condition_mask, axis=axes_I)

# 4. Final step conversion back to a numeric indicator configuration
y_final = tf.cast(exists_condition, dtype=tf.float32)
